match.reason: The bank point covers the same idea but goes deeper than this Year 11 VCE course, with Wien's constant and formula and Planck's energy packets, and cutting those would change its depth rather than make a small adjustment, so a new point is the safer choice.

draft.title: Black body radiation
card: A black body is an ideal object that absorbs all the radiation that hits it. When it is warm, it emits radiation across a range of wavelengths.
The hotter the object, the more energy it emits in total each second. The Stefan-Boltzmann law says this power rises with the fourth power of the temperature in kelvin.

The peak wavelength is the wavelength at which the most energy is emitted. Wien's law says it gets shorter as temperature rises, because peak wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature in kelvin.
Real objects only approximate a black body. A heated piece of metal glows dull red, then orange, then white as its peak moves to shorter wavelengths and more visible light is emitted.
draft.remember: Hotter means more total energy emitted and a shorter peak wavelength.

a.q: A metal rod is heated until its temperature in kelvin doubles. What happens to the radiation it emits?
opts: More energy in total, and a shorter peak wavelength
More energy in total, and a longer peak wavelength
Less energy in total, and a shorter peak wavelength
The same energy in total, and a shorter peak wavelength
a.why: A hotter object emits more energy in total, and its peak moves to a shorter wavelength. The option with a longer peak wavelength reverses Wien's law, which says peak wavelength falls as temperature rises.
a.clue: Think of metal going from red to white as it heats.

b.q: Star P has a surface temperature of 3000 K. Star Q has a surface temperature of 6000 K. Which statement compares their radiation correctly?
opts: Q has a peak wavelength half that of P
Q has a peak wavelength twice that of P
Q has a peak wavelength the same as P
Q has a peak wavelength a quarter that of P
b.why: Peak wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature in kelvin. Doubling the temperature halves the peak wavelength. The option saying twice is tempting, but it treats the two as directly proportional.
b.clue: Peak wavelength and temperature move in opposite directions.

a.best: More energy in total, and a shorter peak wavelength

b.best: Q has a peak wavelength half that of P

problems.detail: "When it is warm, it emits radiation" suggests only warm objects emit. Any object above absolute zero emits thermal radiation, and this matters for the next point, where Earth's surface emits infrared. Better: "At any temperature above absolute zero, it emits radiation across a range of wavelengths."

check.summary: The physics and both answers are correct. One card line implies only warm objects emit radiation, when any object above absolute zero does, so it needs a small rewording.
